objectives: Explain basilar-membrane tonotopy and the place code for frequency.
Contrast the roles of inner and outer hair cells, including the cochlear amplifier.
Describe the traveling wave and the origin of otoacoustic emissions.

slides.title: The traveling wave and tonotopy
slides.body:
When the **stapes** pushes on the **oval window**, it sets the **perilymph** of the cochlea into motion, and the **basilar membrane** ripples in response. **Georg von Bekesy**, using cadaver cochleae and stroboscopic illumination in work that won the **Nobel Prize in 1961**, showed that this motion is not a standing resonance at a single spot but a **traveling wave** that starts at the **base** and sweeps toward the **apex**, growing in amplitude until it reaches a peak and then dying away rapidly.

The location of that peak depends on **frequency**, and this is the heart of cochlear function: **tonotopy**, the orderly mapping of frequency to place. The basilar membrane is not uniform. At the **base**, near the oval window, it is **narrow** (about 0.1 mm) and **stiff**; at the **apex** it is **wide** (about 0.5 mm) and **floppy**. A stiff, light structure resonates at a high frequency; a heavy, compliant one at a low frequency. Consequently, **high frequencies peak near the base** and **low frequencies peak near the apex**. A pure tone of a given frequency therefore excites a specific, narrow region of the membrane, and the brain reads frequency partly from *which* nerve fibers fire, the **place code**. This is why **von Bekesy's** finding underlies clinical facts such as high-frequency loss appearing first in noise and aging: the vulnerable basal region encodes the high frequencies.

The mapping is approximately **logarithmic** in frequency along the length of the cochlea, a relationship captured by the **Greenwood function** (Donald Greenwood, 1961, refined 1990):

$$f = A\,(10^{a x} - k)$$

where $x$ is the fractional distance from the apex and the constants $A \approx 165.4$, $a \approx 2.1$, and $k \approx 0.88$ are fit to the human cochlea with $f$ in hertz. This same equation is used today to program the frequency-to-electrode map of a **cochlear implant** so that electrical stimulation lands at the place the brain expects for each frequency band.

Von Bekesy's passive traveling wave, measured in dead tissue, was beautiful but had a problem: it was too **broad** to explain the exquisite **frequency selectivity** and sensitivity of the living ear. Real ears can distinguish tones differing by a fraction of a percent in frequency and detect motions of the basilar membrane smaller than the diameter of a hydrogen atom. Something **active** must sharpen and amplify the passive wave. That something, we now know, is the **outer hair cells**, and the realization that the cochlea contains a biological amplifier was one of the great surprises of 20th-century sensory physiology, first inferred by **Thomas Gold** in **1948** and confirmed decades later.

slides.title: Inner and outer hair cells
slides.body:
Sitting atop the basilar membrane in the **organ of Corti** are two anatomically and functionally distinct populations of sensory cells. Each human cochlea contains roughly **3500 inner hair cells (IHCs)** arranged in a single row, and roughly **12000 outer hair cells (OHCs)** arranged in three rows. Both bear, on their apical surface, a precise bundle of **stereocilia** graded in height, but they do very different jobs.

The **inner hair cells** are the true **sensory receptors**. They synapse onto about **90-95 percent** of the **afferent** fibers of the auditory nerve, so almost everything the brain learns about sound comes from IHCs. **Mechanoelectrical transduction** works as follows. When the basilar membrane moves, the stereocilia bundle shears against the overlying **tectorial membrane** and tips deflect toward the tallest row. **Tip links**, fine protein filaments discovered by **James Pickles (1984)**, connect the tip of each shorter stereocilium to the side of its taller neighbor; deflection pulls the tip links and yanks open mechanically gated **transduction channels**. **Potassium** flows in from the potassium-rich **endolymph** (driven by the roughly +80 mV **endocochlear potential** that **Bekesy** and later **Tasaki** characterized), depolarizing the cell. Depolarization opens **calcium** channels at the base, triggering **glutamate** release onto the afferent fiber and a train of nerve spikes. The whole transduction step is purely mechanical-to-electrical and fast enough to follow individual cycles at low frequencies, supporting a complementary **temporal code** (phase locking) alongside the place code.

The **outer hair cells** are the **effectors** of the **cochlear amplifier**. They receive mostly **efferent** input (from the brain, via the **olivocochlear bundle**) and possess a remarkable trick: **electromotility**, discovered by **William Brownell** and colleagues in **1985**. When depolarized, an OHC physically **contracts** along its length within microseconds, and when hyperpolarized it elongates. This motion is driven by a dense membrane protein called **prestin**, identified by **Peter Dallos** and colleagues in **2000**. By contracting and elongating in step with the traveling wave, the OHCs pump mechanical energy back into the basilar membrane on a cycle-by-cycle basis, locally boosting its motion by **40-60 dB** for faint sounds and sharpening the tuning to a narrow place. This active feedback is what gives the living cochlea its phenomenal sensitivity and frequency resolution, and it is **nonlinear**: the gain is largest for quiet sounds and shrinks as sounds get louder, which is why loudness grows so steeply once the amplifier saturates. Damage to OHCs (from noise, aging, or ototoxic drugs) removes the amplifier and produces the most common form of sensorineural hearing loss.

slides.title: Otoacoustic emissions: the ear that talks back
slides.body:
Because the outer hair cells actively generate mechanical energy, the cochlea is not a one-way street. Some of that energy travels **backward** out of the cochlea, through the ossicles and eardrum, and into the ear canal, where a sensitive microphone can record it as a faint sound. These sounds are **otoacoustic emissions (OAEs)**, and their discovery was one of the most consequential events in modern audiology.

**David Kemp** reported OAEs in **1978**, placing a sensitive microphone in the sealed ear canal and detecting an echo a few milliseconds after a click stimulus, far too delayed and too narrowband to be a simple acoustic reflection. The only plausible source was an **active**, energy-producing process inside the cochlea, dramatic confirmation of **Thomas Gold's** 1948 conjecture and of the **cochlear amplifier** powered by OHC electromotility. OAEs come in several flavors that clinics use today:

- **Spontaneous OAEs (SOAEs)**: faint tones emitted with no external stimulus, present in many normal ears.
- **Transient-evoked OAEs (TEOAEs)**: the click-evoked echoes Kemp first measured.
- **Distortion-product OAEs (DPOAEs)**: when two tones at frequencies $f_1$ and $f_2$ are played together, the nonlinear amplifier generates a new tone, most prominently at the **cubic distortion product** $2f_1 - f_2$. Measuring its level across frequency probes OHC function place by place.

The clinical power of OAEs is profound for two reasons. First, they are **objective** and require no behavioral response, so they can be measured in a sleeping newborn, an infant, or anyone who cannot reliably press a button. This made OAEs the workhorse of **universal newborn hearing screening**, allowing hearing loss to be caught in the first days of life when early intervention matters most. Second, OAEs are **present only when the outer hair cells are healthy**, so a normal OAE implies a working cochlear amplifier, while absent OAEs flag OHC damage, the signature of typical sensorineural loss.

OAEs also help distinguish where a problem lies. In **auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder**, OAEs are present (OHCs work) but the **auditory brainstem response** is abnormal, localizing the fault to the inner hair cells, the synapse, or the auditory nerve rather than the amplifier. Thus a tiny echo from the ear, predicted by **Gold**, found by **Kemp**, and explained by the electromotility of **Brownell** and the **prestin** of **Dallos**, became one of the most useful objective tests in the entire field, turning the abstract physiology of cochlear mechanics into a five-minute bedside screen.

question.question: Where along the basilar membrane do **high-frequency** sounds produce their peak vibration, and why?
options: At the apex, because the apical membrane is wide and floppy.
At the base, because the basal membrane is narrow and stiff, which resonates best at high frequencies.
Uniformly along the whole membrane, because all frequencies travel together.
At the helicotrema, because that is where the two scalae meet.
question.explanation: Tonotopy follows the mechanical gradient of the basilar membrane. The base is narrow and stiff, so it resonates at high frequencies; the apex is wide and compliant, resonating at low frequencies. Hence high-frequency traveling waves peak near the base (close to the oval window) and low-frequency waves peak near the apex.

hints: Stiff, light structures vibrate fast (high frequency); heavy, floppy ones vibrate slowly.
The base is the stiff narrow end near the oval window.
slides.workedSolution: The basilar membrane stiffens and narrows toward the base and widens and softens toward the apex. Stiff narrow regions resonate at high frequencies, so high tones peak near the base near the oval window; low tones peak at the floppy apex. This is the place code, or tonotopy.

question.question: Interpreting present OAEs with an abnormal ABR.
question.prompt: A newborn passes the otoacoustic-emission screen (clear, robust emissions) but fails the auditory brainstem response, showing absent or grossly abnormal neural waves. Using what you know about which cells generate OAEs versus which structures generate the ABR, reason about where in the auditory pathway the problem most likely lies, and name the disorder this pattern is classically associated with.

question.question: What is the role of **outer hair cells** that distinguishes them from inner hair cells?
options: Outer hair cells carry 95 percent of the afferent auditory-nerve fibers to the brain.

Outer hair cells are the cochlear amplifier: via the protein prestin they change length (electromotility), feeding energy back into the basilar membrane to boost faint sounds by 40-60 dB and sharpen tuning, whereas inner hair cells are the true sensory receptors that drive the afferent nerve.
Outer hair cells detect head rotation and linear acceleration.
Outer hair cells secrete the endolymph that fills the scala media.
question.explanation: Inner hair cells are the primary sensory receptors, synapsing onto roughly 90-95 percent of afferent fibers. Outer hair cells are effectors: their electromotility, driven by prestin (Dallos 2000) and described by Brownell (1985), amplifies and sharpens the traveling wave by 40-60 dB for soft sounds. The other options describe IHCs, vestibular cells, or stria vascularis.

hints: Which cells move (change length) and which cells mainly sense?
The amplifier is built from the protein prestin.
slides.workedSolution: Outer hair cells are the cochlear amplifier. Their electromotility, powered by prestin, lets them contract and elongate in step with the traveling wave, pumping mechanical energy back into the basilar membrane to amplify faint sounds by 40-60 dB and sharpen frequency tuning. Inner hair cells, by contrast, are the sensory receptors that drive almost all of the afferent auditory nerve.

question.question: A distortion-product OAE test plays two tones with $f_1 = 2000$ Hz and $f_2 = 2400$ Hz. At what frequency (in Hz) does the prominent **cubic distortion product** $2f_1 - f_2$ appear?
Why loud sounds grow loud so fast.
question.prompt: A patient with outer-hair-cell damage complains that quiet speech is inaudible but loud speech becomes uncomfortable almost immediately, a small increase in volume seems to jump from too soft to too loud. Using the nonlinear, compressive behavior of the healthy cochlear amplifier and what its loss does to that compression, explain why this narrow comfortable range (recruitment) arises when outer hair cells are damaged.
